ideas.title: Leftover-Offset Check for Square Appointments in BC, Alberta and Manitoba

notes.connected: Connects to the seller's Square account by OAuth, reads future bookings and business hours, and moves bookings back through the Bookings API where the plan allows writes.
notes.engine: The match rule: bookings dated 2026-11-01 to 2027-03-13, saved before the date the owner fixed their time-zone settings and not edited since, flagged when they sit exactly an hour outside business hours.

ideas.summary: For salons, studios and solo providers in BC, Alberta and Manitoba on Square Appointments: finds the bookings still an hour off after the 1 November 2026 time change and moves them back in confirmed batches, until the mismatch ends on 14 March 2027.

public.summary: Find the appointments that are still an hour off since the November time change, and fix them in a few clicks.
public.problem: Your province stopped changing its clocks, and appointments you booked before you updated your settings now show an hour off, in your calendar and in your clients' reminders. Moving them one by one takes hours, and missing one means a client turns up at the wrong time.
public.forWhom: Salons, studios, clinics and solo service providers in British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba who take bookings in Square.
benefits: See every appointment that is still an hour off
Fix them in batches you approve
A checklist to work through if your plan cannot fix them automatically
Fewer wrong-time arrivals and comped services

ideas.problemStatement: Since BC, Alberta and Manitoba moved to permanent daylight time on 1 November 2026, appointments saved before a seller corrected their Square settings sit an hour off; sellers move hundreds by hand and comp services, and Square offers no bulk fix.
ideas.description: A one-off checker. The owner connects Square and enters the date they corrected their location, device and account time zones. The app lists future bookings up to 13 March 2027 that were saved before that date and not edited since, and flags those that fall exactly an hour outside business hours. Where the seller's plan allows API writes (Appointments Plus or Premium), it moves the flagged bookings back in batches the owner confirms; on the free plan it produces a printable checklist. It sends no messages to clients.
ideas.targetCustomer: Salons, studios and solo service providers in British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba on Square Appointments with bookings saved before 1 November 2026.
ideas.whyNow: BC, Alberta and Manitoba moved to permanent daylight time on 1 November 2026 (gov.bc.ca, 2026-10-30); the mismatch with stand-in US zones lasts until 14 March 2027 (HR trade press, 2026-10-19), and Square has no bulk tool.

problemEvidence.summary: Says Square support told them no patch is coming; moving every client an hour by hand, comping appointments, and only halfway through December.

problemEvidence.author: poster F (appointment seller)
problemEvidence.summary: Over 200 appointments affected; peers in Manitoba on other platforms do not have the problem.

review.findings: Re-researched from the watchlist today: no paid job or app for the fix was found (as on 2026-11-20), Calendly shipped the new zones but users still reported wrong times on 2026-11-17, and GoHighLevel leaves existing contacts to the user. The adversarial reviewer cut the total from 21 to 19: reachability 3 to 2 (the only gathering place is Square's moderated community, quiet since 2026-11-10, and the App Marketplace is paused) and feasibility 4 to 3 (Square's Bookings API keeps no time zone, the cutoff differs per seller, and seller-level writes return 403 on the free plan). It found the posters to be independent sellers, that part of the problem is Square's own display and reminder bugs, and that the mismatch ends by itself on 14 March 2027; it recommended not carrying the entry on the watchlist again. Re-scoped to a leftover-offset checker with confirmed batch moves where the plan allows, and a checklist otherwise.

ideas.title: One-Case Disciplinary File for UK Micro Employers

notes.stateful: The owner comes back to one case file over several weeks: timeline, letters, minutes and evidence index.
notes.unattended: A daily job emails the owner before a notice period or the appeal window closes.
notes.engine: The Acas Code's steps in order (investigation, invitation with the right to be accompanied, hearing, outcome, appeal), with skipped steps blocked and working-day deadlines.
notes.shared: The employee receives each letter, and the indexed bundle goes to an adviser or a tribunal; an appeal manager can be a second role.

buildPlan.title: One case, first letter
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, open a case, add dated timeline entries and download the hearing invitation as Word or PDF.
buildPlan.acceptance: A signed-in owner creates a case and downloads an invitation that states the date, time, allegations, enclosed evidence and the right to be accompanied; deployed.

buildPlan.title: Step engine
buildPlan.delivers: The five Acas stages in order, with a step that would be skipped blocked and explained.
buildPlan.acceptance: Tests show no outcome letter can be produced before a hearing record exists and no appeal before an outcome; each stage's letter renders.

buildPlan.title: Evidence log and hearing minutes
buildPlan.delivers: A dated evidence index with capped file uploads and a minutes template with attendees, roles and timestamps.
buildPlan.acceptance: A sample hearing's minutes export to Word with every attendee and role; evidence items list in date order.

buildPlan.title: Deadline reminders
buildPlan.delivers: A scheduled job that emails the owner before notice periods and the appeal window close.
buildPlan.acceptance: A seeded case produces exactly one reminder per due step on the right working day.

buildPlan.title: Hearing bundle
buildPlan.delivers: One-click indexed PDF bundle of the timeline, letters, minutes and evidence index.
buildPlan.acceptance: The bundle's page numbers match its index for a 20-item sample case.

buildPlan.title: Polish and pay per case
buildPlan.delivers: Card payment per case, retention and delete, owner guide, phone layout, keyboard and screen-reader pass, walkthrough test.
buildPlan.acceptance: A walkthrough test runs sign-in to bundle; axe reports no serious issues; deleting a case removes its files.

ideas.summary: For UK owners with under ten staff and no HR adviser: one case file that walks a disciplinary through the Acas Code, writes the letters and minutes, keeps the dates, and exports a hearing bundle, priced per case.

public.summary: Run one staff disciplinary fairly, step by step, with every letter and note kept in one dated file.
public.problem: You have a problem with a member of staff and no HR department. The official guidance is long, each letter has to say the right things, and one missed step can cost you dearly if it goes to a tribunal. From January 2027 far more of your staff will be able to make that claim.
public.forWhom: Owners and managers of small businesses in England, Scotland and Wales who have no HR adviser.
benefits: Always know the next step and what it must include
Letters and meeting notes ready to send
A dated record of what happened and when
A tidy bundle to hand an adviser if it goes further
Pay for one case, not a yearly contract

ideas.problemStatement: Small employers run a disciplinary perhaps once a year, get the steps and letters wrong or pay an outsider to minute or run the hearing; from 1 January 2027 an employee can claim unfair dismissal after six months and the compensation cap goes, so a skipped step costs far more.
ideas.description: A guided case file for one disciplinary, with grievances to follow. The owner opens a case and the app walks through the Acas Code's stages in order (investigation, invitation with the right to be accompanied, hearing, outcome, appeal) and blocks a step that would be skipped. Each stage produces its letter as Word or PDF, the hearing stage gives a minutes template with attendees and roles, and every action is dated in a timeline with an evidence index. Reminders go out before notice periods and the appeal window close, and the file exports as an indexed bundle. It is priced per case, so an owner with one problem does not take a monthly HR platform.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners and managers of micro employers (1 to 10 staff) in England, Scotland and Wales with no HR retainer, no legal-expenses helpline and no membership that includes employment advice: care providers, restaurants, shops, trades.
ideas.buyer: The owner, by card, per case, from the operating budget.
ideas.whyNow: From 1 January 2027 employees can claim unfair dismissal after 6 months instead of 2 years and the compensation limit is removed (Acas, updated 2026-11-12; business.gov.uk, updated 2026-11-15); Acas consulted on a revised disciplinary Code from 30 July to 23 September 2026.

review.findings: Research (19) found that BrightHR, Breathe and CharlieHR list no guided case workflow and that the free Acas templates keep no record or deadlines. The adversarial reviewer found Leo HR, launched 2026-09-02, which guides each stage, keeps a tribunal 'Matter Bundle' and monitors deadlines for small employers at £75 a month, and Adam HR, a freemium letter drafter; it cut competitiveGap from 3 to 2 (total 19 to 18). It also found that both freelance posters bought a person (a note-taker, a hearing officer), not a tool, so they support the need but not software spend, and that the 1 January 2027 date has not moved. Re-scoped to a one-off, per-case disciplinary file for micro employers with no adviser, priced well below a month of Leo HR.

ideas.title: Club-Branded Member Cards with Your Own Numbers for Zeffy

notes.stateful: The club keeps its member register, its own number sequence and one card template per membership type in the app.
notes.connected: Receives each Zeffy membership payment through Zeffy's payment webhook and API using the club's own key, and imports the existing member list by CSV.
notes.unattended: A card is issued and emailed automatically when a membership payment arrives, with a nightly check against Zeffy for missed webhooks.
notes.shared: The administrator designs the card, the member receives it, and partner-club staff check it on a verify page.

buildPlan.title: Import and one card
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, store the club's Zeffy key on the server, import existing members and numbers by CSV, and render a branded PDF card for one member.
buildPlan.acceptance: A 100-row sample list imports with numbers kept; one card shows the club's logo, membership type and number; deployed.

buildPlan.title: Webhook issuing
buildPlan.delivers: Receive Zeffy's payment webhook, drop non-membership payments, assign the next club number and email the card.
buildPlan.acceptance: A test membership payment produces exactly one card email with the next number; a donation produces none; duplicates are ignored.

buildPlan.title: Card designer
buildPlan.delivers: One template per membership type with logo, colours, a leadership signature image and partner or reciprocal logos.
buildPlan.acceptance: Two membership types render different templates from the same register; images stay sharp in the PDF.

buildPlan.title: Verify page and family tiers
buildPlan.delivers: A token-based verify page showing name, type, club number and valid-through date, and one card per named person on family payments.
buildPlan.acceptance: A family payment with three names yields three cards and three verify links; an expired member shows as expired.

buildPlan.title: Polish
buildPlan.delivers: Nightly reconciliation with Zeffy, member list export, data deletion, administrator guide, phone layout, keyboard and screen-reader pass.
buildPlan.acceptance: A walkthrough test runs import to card email; axe reports no serious issues; disconnecting deletes the key and member data.

ideas.summary: For small clubs, museums and associations that sell memberships on Zeffy: member cards in the club's own design, numbered in the club's own sequence and issued automatically on each payment, with a verify page partner clubs can check.

public.summary: Give every member a card in your club's own look, with your own member numbers, sent automatically when they join or renew.
public.problem: Your members pay through Zeffy, but the card they get carries Zeffy's numbers, not yours, and you cannot add your logo, a signature or your partner clubs. So you either redo the cards by hand each season or live with cards that other clubs will not honour.
public.forWhom: Volunteer membership chairs and administrators of small clubs, museums and associations that use Zeffy.
benefits: Cards that look like your club's, not a platform's
Your existing member numbers, carried on
Cards sent automatically on every new payment
A check page your partner clubs can trust

ideas.problemStatement: Clubs on Zeffy cannot customise the membership card: numbers start at one instead of continuing the club's own sequence, and there is no logo, leadership signature or partner-club branding, so cards are redone by hand or not honoured by reciprocal partners.
ideas.description: A small service connected to a club's Zeffy account by its own API key. It imports the existing member list and number sequence, then listens for Zeffy membership payments and issues each new member the next club number and a card in the template set for that membership type: logo, colours, a leadership signature and partner logos. Cards go out by email as PDFs, and each carries a link to a verify page with the club's number and valid-through date. Expiry dates and wallet passes stay with Zeffy, which already handles them.
ideas.targetCustomer: Volunteer membership chairs and administrators of small clubs, museums, historical societies and associations that sell memberships through Zeffy.
ideas.buyer: The organisation, by card, from a small admin budget.
ideas.whyNow: Ten customers commented on Zeffy's card customisation request between 2026-10-23 and about 2026-11-17 (323 votes, open since 2022, no status); Zeffy's API is free and since 2026-09-01 lets an endpoint choose its webhook events.

public.problem: As a registered practice you keep a pile of separate spreadsheets: incidents, complaints, risks, improvements, staff checks and your audit schedule. ideas.problemStatement: Small registered therapy practices keep up to ten unlinked Excel registers with no reminders or escalations, and scramble to assemble evidence for registration and renewal audits; one paid for a custom SharePoint build to fix it.
ideas.description: A register suite that sits beside the practice's existing practice-management software. Clinicians log incidents, and the app runs the reportable-incident clock (24 hours and 5 business days) with state public holidays. Complaints come in through a public form, are acknowledged by email and counted for the statistics the rules require; risks and continuous-improvement items link to them with review-due alerts. A credential register warns before staff qualifications and screening checks expire, an internal audit schedule keeps the year on track, and an evidence pack maps each register to the verification module's clauses for the auditor. Existing Excel or SharePoint registers import by CSV, and records are kept for the 7 years the rules require.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owners and practice managers of NDIS-registered practices for therapeutic supports (registration group 0128) with 2 to 10 clinicians that face verification audits and do not roster support workers.
ideas.buyer: The practice owner, from the admin or compliance budget, flat per practice.
ideas.whyNow: The Practice Standards' verification module for therapeutic supports was compiled again on 2026-07-01; the Securing the NDIS Bill 2026 proposes 7-year payment records and a 90-day claim window; and professional bodies report registration and audits as 'prohibitively costly' (Speech Pathology Australia, 2026).

compliance: Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles: incident and complaint records hold health information about participants, often children; health providers are covered whatever their turnover.
Retention: incident and complaint records must be kept 7 years (incident rules s 12(4), s 25(2); complaints rules s 10(3)); no hard delete, and an exit export.
Data residency (APP 8): confirm the shared Supabase region; Australian hosting is likely expected.

scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: One independent paid job for the task, a one-off SharePoint build (https://www.freelancer.com/api/projects/0.1/projects/40800463/?full_description=true); paid apps exist (https://astalty.com.au/pricing).
scoreRationale.reachability: Search ads and content only, on keywords already served by template packs (https://www.banterspeech.com.au/ndis-templates/).
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: ShiftCare shipped a complaints register in July 2026 (https://shiftcare.com/uk/recent-releases), Astalty has registers with alerts (https://astalty.com.au/features/compliance-dashboard) and Mitti is free for 10 seats (https://mitti.com/pricing).

review.findings: Research (19) found that allied-health practice systems (Splose, Nookal, Cliniko's directory) ship no registers, that CTARS covers them at per-client prices with a AUD 2,500 setup, and that the free NDS register is static. The adversarial reviewer cut the total from 19 to 16: willingnessToPay 4 to 3 (only poster A paid for the task, a one-off SharePoint build; posters B and C paid for consultants), competitiveGap 3 to 2 (ShiftCare shipped a complaints register in July 2026 and a qualifications expiry report in February 2026; Astalty has incident, complaint and risk registers with alerts; Centro maps to the Practice Standards; Mitti is free for up to 10 seats), and complianceBurden 3 to 2 (7-year records of serious incidents about vulnerable people, likely Australian hosting). Re-scoped to practices registered only for therapeutic supports, leading with the reportable-incident clock, the improvement register, the audit schedule and the evidence pack.

gateGap.closedBy: The Australian search-ad test: 8 or more practice sign-ups and 3 price-button clicks at AUD 49 a month would show demand against Astalty and the template packs (reachability 3, competitiveGap 3); a practice manager's dated complaint about keeping audit registers would lift pain to 4.

runNotes.caveats: No candidate cleared the quality gate, so four ideas ship as provisional, each with its gap written on it. Twenty new candidates were scored plus three re-researched watchlist entries; one candidate (Zeffy member cards) looked gate-ready at 22 before research and fell to 17 after research and review. Five candidates were researched by subagents and the two top watchlist entries were researched by the watchlist gatherer; six were adversarially reviewed: one killed (Local Order Status Desk, cheaper apps and free native steps already do it) and five rescored down (time-zone check 21 to 19, disciplinary file 19 to 18, Zeffy cards 19 to 17, charity switch-year pack 20 to 17, NDIS registers 19 to 16). Review went on past three survivors because Zeffy cards ranked above all three before its review. Selection: the time-zone check ranks first at 19 but has willingnessToPay 2 and ends by itself on 2027-03-14 (its reviewer recommended not carrying it on the watchlist again); among the candidates within 2 points, the routine's preferences for willingnessToPay of 3 or more and for small-business buyers put the disciplinary file and the NDIS registers ahead, and Zeffy cards (17, pain 3) took the fourth slot over the charity switch-year pack (17, pain 2, no complaint from its customer), which went to rejectedCandidates. NDIS registers (16) shipped over the two 17s because it has a small-business buyer and is within 2 points of them. Constraints: small-business buyers in ideas 1, 2 and 4; Weekend MVP in idea 1; substantial Multi-week ideas with a buildPlan in 2, 3 and 4; categories at most 2 each. Evidence caveats: idea 1's evidence mixes Square and Calendly users and part of its pain is Square's own display bugs, which the tool cannot fix; idea 3's ten complaints sit in one feature-request thread and count as one item; ideas 2 and 4 rest on paid jobs that bought people (a note-taker, consultants), not software, plus mandates. Saturday's focus sources were thin again: A2 (Open edX, Gibbon, Frappe Education, WordPress LMS forums) was developer and vendor talk; B5 is on the avoid list and C4's HigherEdJobs path returned a 212-byte interstitial and closed postings 404 or 410, so A13 stood in for both. The day's useful veins were freelancer.com (B11), vendor feature boards (feedback.zeffy.com, forums.wildapricot.com), and regulators' pages (gov.uk, legislation.gov.au, irs.gov, federalregister.gov). The run stopped on the account's 5-hour usage limit while the five researchers were starting and resumed at 13:09Z; the researchers were resumed by message, not restarted.
